# Documents in a relational database

`JSONB` stores a whole JSON document in a Postgres column, in a binary form that can be indexed, so
attributes that differ per row and payloads kept exactly as they arrived need no second database.
SQLAlchemy maps each JSONB operator to Python. The rule that catches people out is that a missing key
reads as SQL `NULL`, which quietly changes what a negated filter returns.

## Reading values out

`->` returns JSON and `->>` returns text, and a cast turns that text into a typed value:

| SQL | SQLAlchemy | result |
|---|---|---|
| `payload -> 'k'` | `Event.payload["k"]` | jsonb |
| `payload ->> 'k'` | `Event.payload["k"].astext` | text |
| `payload #>> '{a,b}'` | `Event.payload[("a", "b")].astext` | text, nested |
| `(payload ->> 'k')::int` | `Event.payload["k"].as_integer()` | integer |

Each of these returns `NULL` when the key is missing.

## Containment queries

Most filters use containment, `@>`, which asks whether the document includes a given fragment and
can use a GIN index:

```python
select(Event).where(Event.payload.contains({"user": {"plan": "pro"}}))
```

## Negation and missing keys

Negation is where `NULL` bites. `payload ->> 'device' != 'web'` drops every row that has no
`device` key, because for those rows the comparison is `NULL != 'web'`, which is `NULL` rather than
true. When a missing key should count as "not web", the query has to say so, as in
`or_(Event.payload["device"].astext != "web", ~Event.payload.has_key("device"))`.

## Unnesting arrays

`jsonb_array_elements` turns one row that holds an array into one row per element, after which
`WHERE`, `GROUP BY` and `JOIN` work as usual. In SQLAlchemy, `.table_valued(...)` makes the function
usable in `FROM`, and joining it `ON true` makes Postgres evaluate it laterally, once per row:

```python
item = func.jsonb_array_elements(Event.payload["items"]).table_valued(column("value", JSONB))
select(Event.id, item.c.value["sku"].astext).join(item, true())
```

`jsonb_to_recordset` returns typed columns instead of one `jsonb` value, which saves the casts when
the elements share a shape.

## Paths and updates

Postgres 12 added the SQL/JSON path language, which queries inside one document much as `jq` does.
`$.items[*] ? (@.qty > 1)`, for example, selects the items with a quantity above one.

For updates, `||` merges two documents, `-` removes a key, `#-` removes a path, and
`jsonb_set` writes a value at a path. With `RETURNING`, the same round trip sends back what
changed.

::: {.callout-tip}
## JSONB or columns

Use columns for anything you filter, join or aggregate on routinely, and JSONB for the long tail of
per-row attributes, payloads stored as received, and settings. A GIN index with `jsonb_path_ops`
makes containment fast, but a JSONB key never gets as cheap to query as a typed column.
:::
